messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Salesperson
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Aleksander Novak is a 29-year-old Polish-American man who works as a salesperson for a building materials company, a job that requires him to drive regularly between construction sites and supplier warehouses across the rural outskirts of the city. He presents to therapy approximately fourteen months after surviving a catastrophic flash flood that swept through a campground in the Appalachian foothills where he had been spending a long weekend with two colleagues. The flood arrived in the early hours of the morning with almost no warning — a wall of cold, churning water that tore through the tree line and submerged the lower campground in minutes. Aleksander was woken by shouting, scrambled from his tent into complete darkness, and found himself immediately waist-deep in fast-moving water, unable to see either of his companions, unable to orient himself among the trees he had walked through casually the evening before. He clung to a fence post for what he later estimated was close to two hours before the water receded enough for him to move. One of his colleagues sustained a serious leg injury; the other was unaccounted for for nearly six hours before being found downstream, frightened but physically unharmed. Aleksander himself was not physically injured, a fact he has since found difficult to reconcile with the severity of what he carries.

In the weeks that followed, Aleksander noticed that certain moments would collapse without warning into something that felt less like memory and more like re-entry. He would be standing in a hardware showroom mid-pitch and suddenly be back in the dark water — not picturing it, but inhabiting it, his body braced, his breath short, the fluorescent lights of the warehouse briefly meaningless. What made these episodes particularly disorienting was that they did not always arrive with images. Sometimes there was no picture at all, only the terror itself, arriving full and sourceless, as though the fear had been untethered from its origin and now moved freely through his days. There are stretches of that night he cannot retrieve no matter how deliberately he tries — a gap of perhaps forty minutes between entering the water and reaching the fence post — and this blankness troubles him deeply. When he does attempt to recall the event directly, the terror returns at its original intensity, unchanged by time, and so he has largely stopped trying.

Aleksander now wakes most nights somewhere between two and four in the morning, sitting up and scanning the room before he is fully conscious, checking the window, listening for sounds he cannot name. He moves through his days in a state of low-grade watchfulness that he finds exhausting but cannot switch off. His sales territory includes several routes that pass through wooded, low-lying areas, and on overcast days or after rain, when the ditches alongside the road fill with standing water and the tree canopy closes overhead, he finds the drive nearly intolerable. He has rerouted two of his regular client runs to avoid a particular stretch of highway that passes through a river valley, adding nearly forty minutes to his day. His manager has noticed the scheduling inefficiencies and raised them twice. Aleksander has not explained why.

He had come to believe, with a quiet and settled certainty, that other people could not actually be counted on when things went wrong — that the shouting in the dark, the hours of not knowing, had revealed something true about the fundamental aloneness of crisis. He has declined several social invitations from the colleagues who were present that night and has not spoken to either of them about what happened. He describes feeling like a stranger to himself, as though the person who drove to that campground no longer exists and what remained is someone he does not fully recognise. Nothing he used to find satisfying — the competitiveness of sales, weekend football, his plans to save for a first apartment — seems to carry any weight.

What finally brought Aleksander to seek help was a sales visit two weeks ago to a client whose yard backs onto a creek. He had to pull over on the way home and sit in his car for thirty minutes, unable to account for where the previous hour had gone. He came to therapy not entirely sure what he was hoping for, but most afraid, he said quietly, that this was simply who he was now.
